entry.title: Combined summary - A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean
entry.summary: A recent side project has showcased the integration of a STARK prover within Bitcoin’s consensus mechanism, achieving cryptographic proof over an extensive segment of the blockchain. This demonstration, available for public viewing at [Starked Bitcoin Demo](https://starknet-innovation.github.io/starked-bitcoin/) with open-source code at [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/starknet-innovation/starked-bitcoin), presents a single 1.6 MB proof file (“seal”) verifiable in roughly half a second by modern browsers. The proof encapsulates three pivotal assertions: validation of the header chain from genesis to the current tip in accordance with Bitcoin Core's mainnet rules (excluding only the wall-clock time-too-new rule), full replay of blocks 935,001 through 972,500 with rigorous enforcement of block and transaction structure, and confirmation of the resulting UTXO set aligning with Bitcoin Core’s `hash_serialized` at block 972,500. This is further strengthened by a Merkle root commitment over the UTXO set, enabling compact inclusion or non-inclusion proofs for specific outpoints—features facilitated directly within the demo environment. The construction deliberately omits script validation and signature checks, adopting trust assumptions similar to those underlying assumevalid, yet includes all witness data to allow future retrofitting of script verification without reconstructing previous proofs. It starts from Bitcoin Core’s assumeUTXO snapshot at block 935,000, verifying the initial state against the chain parameters and covering preceding blocks via their headers alone. This approach reflects the practical constraints of computational resources, as generating a full-from-genesis proof would be significantly more demanding—estimated at approximately 325 H100 GPU hours. Notably, this project remains unaudited and actively invites external review. The technical foundation leverages Stwo, a circle STARKs implementation over M31, interfaced through a Zig port ([Stwo-Zig](https://github.com/teddyjfpender/stwo-zig)), and utilizes CUDA acceleration to produce byte-identical proofs. Large block proving is notably efficient, taking just under three seconds for blocks with 2^23 trace rows on an H100 GPU. Proof aggregation occurs recursively by epoch, culminating in a unified proof that binds together headers, blocks, and the UTXO set. Circuits are specified with Lean 4, whose formal constraints guide the Zig-based prover, and are rigorously tested for specification fidelity against Bitcoin Core’s C++ logic using extensive differential fuzz testing. The verification process upholds high confidence in behavioral alignment with Bitcoin Core, despite not constituting formal equivalence proofs. Trust is placed in the fundamental soundness of the employed cryptographic primitives (Stwo/FRI/LogUp), the Fiat–Shamir heuristic in the random oracle model—including recursive applications as examined in [this delvingbitcoin.org thread](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/block-wide-signature-aggregation-via-snarks/2875)—and a compact set of native verifier checks. Comprehensive documentation distinguishing proven aspects from trusted assumptions is maintained in [verification.md](https://github.com/starknet-innovation/starked-bitcoin/blob/a3e06f53f8b28310933265540e8b4189fe630f66/docs/reference/verification.md). As a tangible outcome, the verify-snapshot tool enables users to validate assumeUTXO snapshots—such as those produced by Core’s dumptxoutset—against the seal, affirming critical figures like base block, coin count, total amount, and hash_serialized. On standard hardware, verification was demonstrated to process a 9.39 GB snapshot containing over 164 million coins in seventy-two seconds, while consuming only 0.5 GB RAM. A deeper consideration reveals that the bulk of verification time (70.7 out of 72 seconds) is consumed by reading the snapshot from disk to recompute its hash, with the actual cryptographic proof verifying in about half a second in-browser via WebAssembly. Wrapping the proof in a Groth16 zkSNARK could reduce data size but offers minimal further speedup, and would introduce a trusted setup, foregoing the STARK’s post-quantum security properties. The current proof structure thus preserves both efficiency and robust security assumptions. Analyses of the proof system highlight the importance of precise header validation—encompassing proof of work, median time checks, and block version signaling—which remains lightweight and verifiable by light clients independently of zero-knowledge methods. Commitments to per-block undo data, along with UTXO set updates, form a resilient strategy for block validation. This methodology presumes established knowledge of block headers and a committed UTXO set prior to the validation sequence, with each block’s undo data encoding the specific spent coins and transaction order.
